turns.speaker: A
turns.text: Imagine two runners in a marathon. The first starts fast, feels great for the first half, then slows down a lot. The second starts a little slower, then runs the second half faster than the first. The second runner has run a negative split. Many coaches say this is the smartest way to race.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: A negative split means that the second half of a race is faster than the first. An even split, with both halves at the same pace, is also a good result. The opposite, a positive split, means slowing down in the second half. This is the most common pattern among recreational runners.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: Why is starting slower better? One reason is glycogen preservation. When you run too fast early, you burn your limited carbohydrate stores quickly. By starting at a controlled pace, you save fuel for the end of the race.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: Another reason is aerobic efficiency. At a sustainable pace, your body produces energy mainly with oxygen, which is efficient. If you go too fast, more energy comes from systems that cause fatigue to build up faster.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: A good pacing strategy also helps mentally. Passing other runners in the last ten kilometers feels wonderful. Being passed feels terrible.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: In practice, a slight negative split is a good goal. Start a few seconds per kilometer slower than your target pace, and speed up gradually once you feel settled.
